newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey central bank sees 1996 inflation at 80 pct.
newsitem.headline: Turkey central bank sees 1996 inflation at 80 pct.

text.p: Turkish Central Bank Governor Gazi Ercel said on Wednesday the bank would continue to implement monetary policies to prevent 1996 inflation from rising over its forecast of 80 percent.

"I would like to stress that the Central Bank will take pains with limits and developments on monetary indicators and continue to implement a monetary policy which will not cause any further rise in inflation, which we forecast at 80 percent for this year," Ercel said in written remarks prepared for Reuters.
He did not make clear whether he meant wholesale or consumer price inflation.
Turkey's July year-on-year inflation was 81.2 percent in consumer prices and 76.3 percent in wholesale prices.

"It is estimated that the budget will give a surplus of two percent of GNP (gross national product) excluding interest payments in 1996," he said. Last year the ratio of primary bugdet surplus to GNP was 3.4 percent.
"The ultimate goal of the Central Bank is to reduce inflation to single digits and keep it there. This is doubtlessly not a matter that the Central Bank can realise alone," Ercel said.
"Macroeconomic policies should be drawn up in an anti-inflationary way which can be achieved through a credible medium-term programme that targets lowering inflation."
Ercel said the Central Bank's monetary programme aimed at curbing inflation by restraining growth in money supplies. "The implementation of monetary policy requires fine tuning," he said.

He said the Central Bank had used open market operations and foreign currency transactions to counter "significant fluctuations" in monetary indicators caused by the government's higher-than-expected civil servant pay rises and the treasury's reliance on Central Bank funds for payments worth 75 trillion lira ($869 million) in July.
Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's Islamist-led government gave a 50 percent pay rise to civil servants in July shortly after it came to power.
The treasury, which did not borrow from domestic markets because of concerns over the new government's economic policies had drawn cash from the Central Bank to finance July payments.
Ercel said the relationship between the Central Bank and the treasury was now "constructive".
